title: Cell-sized skeletal elements are shaped by molecular forces, large ones by mechanics

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Cell-sized skeletal elements are shaped by molecular forces, large ones by mechanics

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Skeletal elements comparable in size to a single cell (sponge spicules, radiolarian and foraminiferal skeletons) are shaped by molecular forces such as surface tension, whereas massive skeletons such as vertebrate bones are shaped by gravity, muscle action and mechanical loads, so scale produces essential differences in their controlling forces and forms.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The effect of _scale_, then, of which we had so much to say in our introductory chapter on Magnitude, is bound to be apparent in the study of skeletal fabrics, and to lead to essential differences between the big and the little, the massive and the minute, in regard to their controlling forces and their resultant forms.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IX, “On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons”; topic “Classification of skeletal forms by scale”. Scope: skeletal elements of all sizes, from protist skeletons and spicules to vertebrate bones

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch09-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.52

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Scaling predictions are measurable, but 'molecular forces' is broad and requires modern reinterpretation. Morphological data support a comparative test, yet confounding and sparse microscopic taxa limit a clean general conclusion.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across skeletal elements spanning orders of magnitude, estimate geometric scaling of surface, gravitational and loading stresses and compare form with predicted dominant-force regimes. Support requires a reproducible size transition from surface- or molecular-force signatures to load-adapted geometry.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Material composition, phylogeny and function covary with scale.

Force dominance is inferred rather than directly observed.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Scale is measurable and the two regimes suggest different geometries, but the forces themselves are an interpretation of those geometries. Open scans cover large bones well and minute skeletons poorly, so only a biased slice of the size range can be compared. Even a clean size trend would leave material and ancestry as alternative explanations of the form difference.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Place skeletal elements on a size axis and test whether forms near cell size match surface-tension geometries while large bones match load trajectories, using curvature, junction angles and stress-alignment metrics. A change of regime with size supports the claim; the same controlling geometry at both scales refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Surface tension versus muscle and gravity has to be inferred from form, and several mappings are possible.

Phylogeny and material change with size, and cell-sized spicules are scarce in CT archives built for bones.
